title: Starship Reaches Orbit for First Time, but Returns Early
paragraphs: SpaceX's Starship reached orbit for the first time on September 28, carrying 26 new Starlink internet satellites into space. But an engine problem cut the flight short, bringing the spacecraft back to Earth hours earlier than planned.

The 124-meter rocket lifted off from Starbase in Texas on its 14th full-scale flight. One of the spacecraft's engines shut down earlier than expected during the ascent. Flight controllers spent several tense minutes assessing whether it could continue safely before giving the go-ahead to enter orbit. Cheers erupted when Mission control announced, "Starship is orbital."

Once in orbit, the spacecraft released the satellites one by one. It was the first time Starship had delivered operational satellites, showing what the rocket could do beyond test flights. SpaceX hopes to use it to carry large numbers of satellites into space as it expands its Starlink internet network.

The original plan called for six laps around Earth over nearly 10 hours, followed by a splashdown in the Pacific near Chile. Because of the engine trouble, SpaceX brought the spacecraft back after about three hours instead. It splashed down north of Hawaii, then tipped over and burst into flames.
The first-stage booster had already separated and splashed down in the Gulf of Mexico as planned.

Earlier Starship tests had reached space, but none had completed an orbit. This flight was therefore a major step toward SpaceX's goal of making the giant rocket fully reusable. On future flights, the company hopes to catch the returning spacecraft with mechanical arms at the launch site so it can fly again.

Starship also has a potential role in NASA's plans to return astronauts to the moon. Artemis III, planned for 2027, will test docking between NASA's Orion spacecraft and commercial lunar landers in Earth orbit. NASA aims to land astronauts on the moon on the following mission, using a lander from SpaceX or Blue Origin.
